title: Enums and Literal Types
summary: A literal type allows one exact value. A union can allow a short list of exact choices.
introduction: A literal type allows one exact value. A union can allow a short list of exact choices. A game move might be only "left" or "right". Describe a small set of choices, then compare that with an enum, a named group of values.
learningObjectives: Declare numeric and string enums and read the JavaScript they compile to
Model a fixed set of options with a literal union or an as const object instead
Explain why enums fail under erasableSyntaxOnly and Node's type stripping

blocks.text: An `enum` declares a set of named constants. Without explicit values the members count up from 0, and the compiled object maps both ways: `Direction.Left` is `2` and `Direction[2]` is `"Left"`. Since TypeScript 5.0 every enum is a *union enum*: the type `Direction` accepts only its four members, so an arbitrary number is rejected.

blocks.title: numeric.ts
npx tsc numeric.ts
blocks.content:
numeric.ts:11:1 - error TS2322: Type '42' is not assignable to type 'Direction'.

11 heading = 42;
   ~~~~~~~


Found 1 error in numeric.ts:11

blocks.text: The `console.log` line prints `0 Left 2`. Unlike interfaces and type aliases, an enum produces real JavaScript. Here is what `tsc` emits for `Direction`: an object built inside a function, with the reverse mapping created by the double assignment.

blocks.title: numeric.js (emitted by tsc)

blocks.text: Giving every member a string value makes logs, JSON and database rows readable (`"info"` instead of `1`). String enums have no reverse mapping and are *nominal*: even the exact string `"info"` is not accepted where `LogLevel` is expected. You must write `LogLevel.Info`.

blocks.title: string-enum.ts
npx tsc string-enum.ts
blocks.content:
string-enum.ts:12:5 - error TS2345: Argument of type '"info"' is not assignable to parameter of type 'LogLevel'.

12 log("info", "server started");
       ~~~~~~


Found 1 error in string-enum.ts:12

blocks.text: Whether that strictness is a feature or a nuisance depends on where the values come from. For a value typed inside your own code it prevents typos; for a value parsed from a request body you would have to convert the string to the enum member first anyway.

A union of string literals (`"debug" | "info" | "error"`) gives the same compile-time safety with zero runtime code, and plain strings are accepted. When you also need the list at runtime, for a dropdown or validation, declare an `as const` object once and derive the union from it with `typeof` and `keyof`, so the two can never drift apart.

blocks.title: literal.ts
npx tsc literal.ts
blocks.content:
literal.ts:15:5 - error TS2345: Argument of type '"trace"' is not assignable to parameter of type 'LogLevel'.

15 log("trace", "too chatty");
       ~~~~~~~


Found 1 error in literal.ts:15

blocks.text: The two valid calls print `[info] cache warmed` and `[error] disk full`. Read the type line slowly: `typeof LOG_LEVELS` is the object type, `keyof` of that is `"Debug" | "Info" | "Error"`, and indexing the object type with those keys yields the union of the values. `as const` is essential; without it every value would widen to `string` and the union would collapse to `string`.

Everything else in this tutorial so far could be deleted from the source to obtain valid JavaScript. An enum cannot: it *is* runtime code. TypeScript 5.8 added the `erasableSyntaxOnly` option to flag such constructs, and Node.js 24, which runs `.ts` files by stripping types, refuses them with the error code `ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX`.

blocks.title: npx tsc --erasableSyntaxOnly erasable.ts
blocks.content:
erasable.ts:1:6 - error TS1294: This syntax is not allowed when 'erasableSyntaxOnly' is enabled.

1 enum Status {
       ~~~~~~


Found 1 error in erasable.ts:1

blocks.title: Common mistake: expecting enums to disappear like types
blocks.text: Teams that adopt `node app.ts` or a build tool that only strips types see enums fail at startup, not at compile time. The same applies to `namespace` blocks with values and to constructor parameter properties. If any part of your toolchain relies on type stripping, enable `"erasableSyntaxOnly": true` so the compiler reports these constructs where they are written, and prefer literal unions or `as const` objects.

A `const enum` is inlined: every `Flag.On` in the source becomes the literal `1 /* Flag.On */` in the output and no object is emitted. That removes the runtime cost but makes the enum invisible to other tools, and with `isolatedModules` (which the 5.9 `tsc --init` template enables) the compiler emits a const enum as an ordinary enum object anyway, so the saving disappears. Most teams avoid them.

rows: A fixed set of string options checked by the compiler
The same, plus the list of values at runtime
`as const` object and a derived union
Names for numeric flags or codes from an external protocol

blocks.title: Default choice
blocks.text: Start with a literal union. Move to an `as const` object when you need to iterate the values. Reach for `enum` only when you want the reverse mapping of numeric codes or nominal typing, and then keep in mind that it is runtime code.

questions.question: Given `enum Color { Red, Green = 5, Blue }`, what is `Color.Blue`?
questions.explanation: Members without an initialiser continue counting from the previous member. Red is 0, Green is set to 5, so Blue is 6.

questions.question: A union of string literals such as `"debug" | "info"` produces no JavaScript at all after compilation.
questions.explanation: Type aliases and literal unions exist only in the type system. Enums, by contrast, compile to a real object.

seo.title: TypeScript Enums vs Literal Types and as const
seo.description: Learn numeric and string enums, what they compile to, the literal-union and as const alternatives, const enums, and why enums break Node.js type stripping.
